(Section)

That is, do not speak until he speaks, do not command until he commands, do not issue a legal ruling (fatwa) until he issues one, and do not decide a matter until he is the one who judges it and enforces it. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "Do not say anything contrary to the Book and the Sunnah (the Prophet's teachings and practice)." Al-ʿAwfī narrated from him, who said: "They were forbidden to speak in front of his words."

The comprehensive statement on the meaning of the verse is: do not hasten with any statement or action before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) says or does something.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, and do not speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds become worthless while you do not perceive.﴾ (al-Ḥujurāt: 2)

If raising their voices above his voice is a cause of their deeds becoming worthless, then how about putting forward their own opinions, intellects, tastes, political views, and knowledge over what he brought, and elevating them above it? Is this not more deserving of rendering their deeds worthless?

(Section)

Among the etiquette toward the Messenger (ﷺ) is that one should not go ahead of him with any command, prohibition, permission, or disposal, until he himself commands, prohibits, or permits, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger.﴾

This remains in effect until the Day of Resurrection and has not been abrogated. Thus, going ahead of his Sunnah after his death is like going ahead of him during his lifetime, and there is no difference between the two for anyone of sound intellect.

Mujāhid, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Do not decide matters on behalf of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

Abū ʿUbayda said: The Arabs say, "Do not go ahead of the imam, or ahead of the father," meaning: do not hasten with a command or prohibition without him.

Others said: "Do not command until he commands; do not forbid until he forbids."

Among the etiquette toward him is that voices should not be raised above his voice. For it is a cause of deeds becoming worthless, so what is to be thought of raising opinions and the products of thoughts above his Sunnah and what he brought? Do you think that this would bring about the acceptance of deeds, while raising one's voice above his voice brings about their nullification?

(Section)

The sound heart is the one that is free from having any form of association with Allah in it, in any way. Rather, its servitude is purely for Allah, the Exalted, in will, love, reliance, turning in repentance, humility, fear, and hope. And its deeds are purified for Allah: if it loves, it loves for the sake of Allah; if it hates, it hates for the sake of Allah; if it gives, it gives for the sake of Allah; and if it withholds, it withholds for the sake of Allah. But this alone is not sufficient until it is free from submission to and judgment by anyone other than the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, so that it firmly binds its heart to him, following and emulating him alone, above everyone else, in statements and actions. This covers the statements of the heart, which are beliefs, and the statements of the tongue, which are reports of what is in the heart; and the actions of the heart, which are will, love, dislike, and their consequences; and the actions of the limbs.

Thus, the one who judges over all of this, in its smallest and greatest matters, is what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. So one does not go ahead of him with any belief, statement, or action, as Allah, the Exalted, said:

﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger.﴾ (al-Ḥujurāt: 1)

That is, do not say until he says, and do not act until he commands. One of the early generations (salaf) said: "No act, however small, is without two registers being opened for it: Why? And how?" That is: Why did you do it? And how did you do it?

The first is a question about the cause, motive, and driving force of the act: is it an immediate personal benefit of the doer, an aim of worldly purposes, such as the love of people's praise or fear of their blame, or the attainment of an immediately desired thing or the repelling of an immediately disliked thing?

Or is the motive for the act the fulfillment of the right of servitude, seeking closeness and nearness to the Lord, the Glorified and Exalted, and seeking a means of approach to Him?

The point of this question is: Was it incumbent upon you to do this act for your Master, or did you do it for your own pleasure and desire?

The second is a question about following the Messenger, peace be upon him, in that act of worship: was that deed something I legislated for you through my Messenger, or was it a deed I did not legislate and did not approve?

The first is a question about sincerity, and the second about following, for Allah, the Glorified, does not accept any deed unless both are present.

The way to be free of the first question is by purifying sincerity.

The way to be free of the second question is by realizing following, and the heart's soundness from a will that contradicts sincerity and a desire that contradicts following.

This is the reality of the soundness of the heart, for which salvation and happiness are guaranteed.

Abu 'Amr said: Hisham ibn 'Ammar narrated from Sadaqah ibn Khalid, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir told us, who said: 'Ata' al-Khurasani told me, who said: The daughter of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas told me, and she said: When the verse was revealed: "O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet"

**[Section: On the expedition of ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn al-Fazārī against the Banū Tamīm]**

Mention of the expedition (sariyya, a raid led by a small detachment) of ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn al-Fazārī against the Banū Tamīm. This was in Muḥarram of this year. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent him against them with a force of fifty horsemen, none of whom were Muhajirun (emigrants from Makkah) or Ansar (helpers from Madinah). He would travel by night and lie in ambush by day. He attacked them in an open plain while they had sent out their livestock to pasture. When they saw the force, they fled. He took from them eleven men, twenty-one women, and thirty children, and drove them to Madinah, where they were lodged in the house of Rumla bint al-Ḥārith. Then a number of their chiefs came to plead for them: ʿUṭārid ibn Ḥājib, al-Zibriqān ibn Badr, Qays ibn ʿĀṣim, al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, Qays ibn al-Ḥārith, Nuʿaym ibn Saʿd, ʿAmr ibn al-Ahtam, and Rabāḥ ibn al-Ḥārith. When they saw their women and offspring, they wept to them and hastened (to the Prophet). They came to the door of the Prophet (ﷺ) and called out: "O Muhammad, come out to us!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out, and Bilal called the prayer. They clung to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and spoke to him. He stood with them, then went on and prayed Ẓuhr. Then he sat in the courtyard of the mosque. They put forward ʿUṭārid ibn Ḥājib, who spoke and delivered a sermon. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) instructed Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās, who responded to them. Allah revealed concerning them:

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the private chambers, most of them do not reason. And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 4–5]

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned to them their captives and their prisoners. Then al-Zibriqān, the poet of the Banū Tamīm, stood up and recited boastfully:

*We are the noble ones; no tribe can equal us.*
*From among us are kings, and among us are the churches raised.*

*How many of the tribes, all of them, have we subdued,*
*in plunder, and the excellence of honour is followed.*

*We feed the guest at times of drought,*
*with roast meat when the clouds bring no rain.*

*People's chiefs come to us*
*from every far land, and we receive them honourably.*

*We slaughter the she-camels, whole, in our stock,*
*for those who arrive, and they are sated when they are lodged.*

*You will never see us go to a tribe we boast against*
*without their gaining from us, and they become the head that is cut off.*

*Whoever boasts against us in that, we know him,*
*so the people return, and the reports are heard...*

*We have refused, and no one can refuse on our behalf.*
*Thus, when it comes to boasting, we rise high.*

Then Ḥassān ibn Thābit, the poet of Islam, stood up and answered him extemporaneously:

*Indeed, the foremost of Fihr and their brethren*
*have established a custom for people to follow.*

*Everyone whose inner nature is the fear of God is pleased with it,*
*and all good that is done.*

*They are a people who, when they fight, harm their enemy,*
*and when they seek to benefit their allies, they benefit them.*

*That is their disposition, not something newly invented;*
*know that the worst of dispositions are innovations.*

*If there are any among the people who outstrip, after them,*
*every outstripping is a follower of their lesser outstripping.*

*The people cannot mend what their hands have torn,*
*in defence, nor can they tear what they have mended.*

*If they race the people one day, their advance wins,*
*or if they weigh themselves against people of glory, they are equal in generosity.*

*Chaste, whose chastity is mentioned in revelation;*
*they do not sully themselves, nor does greed destroy them.*

*They do not withhold their bounty from a neighbour,*
*and no stain of covetousness touches them.*

*When we set upon a tribe, we do not creep up on them*
*as the cub creeps toward the wild beast.*

*We rise up when war reaches us with its claws,*
*when the lesser ones among its talons are humbled.*

*They do not boast when they overcome their enemy,*
*and if they are struck, there is no injustice or panic.*

*As if in battle, with death having closed in,*
*they are lions in a thicket at whose wrists are bracelets.*

*Take from them what they grant willingly when they are angered,*
*and do not let your concern be the matter they refused.*

*For in fighting them, leave off enmity with them;*
*it is an evil through which poison and bitterness are tasted.*

*How honourable is a people whose partisans are the Messenger of God,*
*when desires and factions diverge.*

*My praise, offered to them, is from a heart that supports it,*
*and in what it loves, a tongue that weaves and composes.*

*Indeed, they are the best of all living people,*
*if the people's serious speech is at its most serious, or they become silent.*

When Ḥassān had finished, al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis said: "Indeed, this man is supported (by his people). His orator is more eloquent than our orator, his poet is more skilled than our poet, and their voices are higher than our voices." Then they embraced Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them their gifts, and he gave them generously.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 49, verse 6:

"It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to the Banu al-Mustaliq after the battle as a collector of zakat (sadaqat).
